sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a non-parametric framework for Bayesian inference, allowing for both predictions and uncertainty estimates. The flexibility of GPs comes from their kernel functions, which encode prior assumptions about function structure.

However, the expressiveness of a standard GP is limited by its kernel (Pravesh and Roi 2020). Choosing an appropriate kernel often requires domain expertise and trial and error, and a fixed kernel may fail to capture the complex, multi-scale structure present in real data. This motivated Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) (Damianou and Lawrence 2013), which compose multiple GP layers into a hierarchy that can learn rich representations automatically.

DGPs stack multiple GP layers so that each layer’s output becomes the next layer’s input. This composition allows the model to learn features at multiple levels of abstraction — much like deep neural networks — while retaining the principled uncertainty quantification of the GP framework. The price of this flexibility is tractability: although each layer is individually Gaussian, the composition produces a non-Gaussian joint distribution over latent functions, making exact inference intractable.

This dissertation provides an exploration of Gaussian Processes and Deep Gaussian Processes. We begin by deriving standard GP regression from first principles, show how composing these GPs into deep layered hierarchies leads to greater expressiveness at the cost of tractability, and then develop the variational inference needed to train these models at scale.

Finally, we apply DGPs and GPs to real-world datasets within finance, both credit-card default prediction and mortgage default prediction. We discuss advantages, limitations and tradeoffs between DGP structures, and demonstrate their ability to capture complex patterns and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates that are crucial for risk based decision making. We compare GP based models to classical machine learning (ML) models, and show that GP based models lead to better calibrated uncertainty estimates.
We begin by deriving the theory of standard GPs.

sec.title: 2. Towards Gaussian Processes
sec.p: The problem in supervised machine learning is inferring functional relationships between input variables and observed outputs from a set of training examples. Given dataset \mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n𝒟={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n where \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^D𝐱i∈ℝD is an input vector and y_i \in \mathbb{R}yi∈ℝ is the corresponding output, we aim to learn some function f: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}f:ℝD→ℝ that represents the underlying mapping y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \epsilony=f(𝐱)+ϵ, where \epsilonϵ is a noise term.

In a classical frequentist approach, we typically define the function ff as a parametric model and estimate it by using a finite set of parameters \mathbf{w}𝐰. For example, in linear regression we have f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}f(𝐱)=𝐰⊤𝐱, and we aim to find the best estimate \hat{\mathbf{w}}𝐰̂ such that y_i \approx \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top \mathbf{x}_iyi≈𝐰̂⊤𝐱i for all ii. Within Bayesian statistics, we place a prior distribution on the parameters \mathbf{w}𝐰, and then compute a posterior distribution p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})p(𝐰∣𝒟) that captures updated beliefs about the parameters after observing the data (Bishop 2006; Murphy 2013).

In these so-called parametric models, the function ff is fully specified by a finite set of parameters \mathbf{w}𝐰. This number and structure of parameters is fixed in advance, and therefore the function space of ff is limited by the choice of model. Further to this, the choice of parameters is often required before observing the data, and therefore requires domain expertise to select an appropriate model.

In contrast to frequentist approaches that specify a parametric model and estimate its parameters via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) (Bishop 2006), GPs place a prior directly on an infinite-dimensional function space (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; D. J. MacKay 1998; Williams and Rasmussen 1995). Observed data then reduces uncertainty, yielding a final posterior distribution that captures the updated beliefs about the function.
This section outlines the theory of GPs for regression tasks, starting from the weight-space view of Bayesian linear regression and building up to the function-space view of GPs.

sec.title: 2.1 The Weight Space View
sec.p: Before moving to the full function space perspective, it is helpful to build intuition through a finite-dimensional parametric approach. The weight space view treats regression as Bayesian inference over a weight vector. We show how the the structure of the resulting predictive distribution can be expressed in terms of inner products between inputs, which naturally motivates the transition into Gaussian processes (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; D. J. MacKay 1998).

We begin with a linear model of the form
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{w}, \qquad(1)f(𝐱)=𝐱⊤𝐰,(1)

where \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^D𝐰∈ℝD is a weight vector. To make this more general, we consider an expansion of basis functions (Bishop 2006)
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j \phi_j(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{w}, \qquad(2)f(𝐱)=∑j=1Mwjϕj(𝐱)=𝛟(𝐱)⊤𝐰,(2)

where \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = [\phi_1(\mathbf{x}), \ldots, \phi_M(\mathbf{x})]^\top𝛟(𝐱)=[ϕ1(𝐱),…,ϕM(𝐱)]⊤ is a vector of basis functions, which maps the input to an MM-dimensional feature space, with weights \mathbf{w} = [w_1, \ldots, w_M]^\top𝐰=[w1,…,wM]⊤. This becomes more general than the simple linear model, allowing the modeling of non-linear relationships through the choice of basis functions \phi_j(\cdot)ϕj(⋅), without breaking linearity in the parameters \mathbf{w}𝐰.

Given some training data \mathcal{D}𝒟, our goal is to learn a set of weights \mathbf{w}𝐰 that best describes the data - which we call \hat{\mathbf{w}}𝐰̂. A common approach is to use maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) (Bishop 2006; Murphy 2013), which finds the single best set of weights that maximises the likelihood of the observed data. However, this ignores how it is possible for different weight vectors to explain the observed data equally well, but make very different predictions in unobserved region. MLE can also lead to overfitting, where the model fits the training data too closely and fails to generalise to new data.
This motivates a Bayesian approach.

sec.title: 2.2.1 Prior and Likelihood
sec.p:
A Bayesian approach addresses these issues by placing a prior distribution over \mathbf{w}𝐰, which turns the the problem into so-called Bayesian linear regression (Bishop 2006; Gelman et al. 2025). A natural choice is a zero-mean Gaussian prior:
p(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \Sigma_p), \qquad(3)p(𝐰)=𝒩(𝐰∣𝟎,Σp),(3)

where \Sigma_p \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times M}Σp∈ℝM×M is the prior covariance matrix. A common prior is \Sigma_p = \sigma_w^2 \mathbf{I}Σp=σw2𝐈, which gives independent, identically distributed, (i.i.d.) Gaussian weights with variance \sigma_w^2σw2 (D. J. C. MacKay 1992).

When modelling each observation as y_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \epsilon_iyi=f(𝐱i)+ϵi, where \epsilon_iϵi is independent noise \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)ϵi∼𝒩(0,σn2), we get a likelihood for a single observation of the form
p(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(y_i \mid \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2). \qquad(4)p(yi∣𝐱i,𝐰)=𝒩(yi∣𝛟(𝐱i)⊤𝐰,σn2).(4)

Assuming that there is independence across observations, and conditioning on \mathbf{w}𝐰, we have that the joint likelihood over \mathcal{D}𝒟 becomes
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{N}(y_i \mid \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2). \qquad(5)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)=∏i=1n𝒩(yi∣𝛟(𝐱i)⊤𝐰,σn2).(5)

Collecting observations into the design matrix \Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times M}Φ∈ℝn×M with \Phi_{ij} = \phi_j(\mathbf{x}_i)Φij=ϕj(𝐱i) (Rasmussen and Williams 2008) (see Appendix 6.3 for the explicit construction), Equation 5 becomes a single multivariate Gaussian rather than a product of univariate Gaussians:
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \Phi \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}). \qquad(6)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)=𝒩(𝐲∣Φ𝐰,σn2𝐈).(6)

sec.title: 2.2.2 Posterior over Weights
sec.p:
Applying Bayes’ theorem to this gives the posterior distribution over weights:
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w})}{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X})}. \qquad(7)p(𝐰∣𝐗,𝐲)=p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)p(𝐰)p(𝐲∣𝐗).(7)

Because the Gaussian prior is a product of Gaussians, and the likelihood is also Gaussian, the posterior is Gaussian as well (Bishop 2006; Bernardo and Smith 2000). The prior and likelihood are conjugate distributions, so the posterior is in the same family as the prior, this is called conjugacy (Gelman et al. 2025) and is a property that allows for closed-form inference. Evaluating the posterior gives covariance

The posterior distribution over the weights is therefore
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \bar{\mathbf{w}}, \Sigma_w). \qquad(10)p(𝐰∣𝐗,𝐲)=𝒩(𝐰∣𝐰‾,Σw).(10)

sec.p:

sec.title: 2.4 From Weight Space to Function Space
sec.p:
The predictive distribution in Equation 12 is expressed in terms of the feature map \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟. However, we can see \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟 appears only through inner products with the posterior covariance \Sigma_wΣw, of the form \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \Sigma_p \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}')𝛟(𝐱)⊤Σp𝛟(𝐱′). We can define this kernel function (interchangeably called a covariance function) as an inner product in the feature space: (Schölkopf 2002; Rasmussen and Williams 2008)
k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \Sigma_p \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}'), \qquad(13)k(𝐱,𝐱′)=𝛟(𝐱)⊤Σp𝛟(𝐱′),(13)
which measures similarity between inputs in the feature space, weighted by the prior covariance \Sigma_pΣp.

With this definition, we can collect all pairwise kernel evaluations over the full training set into the kernel matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}K∈ℝn×n with K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)Kij=k(𝐱i,𝐱j), and the vector of cross-covariances \mathbf{k}_* \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐤*∈ℝn with [\mathbf{k}_*]_i = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_*)[𝐤*]i=k(𝐱i,𝐱*). This allows for rewriting the predictive equation entirely in terms of the kernel. This can be done by reparametrizing the posterior covariance \Sigma_w = (\sigma_n^{-2}\Phi^\top\Phi + \Sigma_p^{-1})^{-1}Σw=(σn−2Φ⊤Φ+Σp−1)−1 using the matrix inversion lemma (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, Equation A.9),
(A + UCV)^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U\bigl(C^{-1} + VA^{-1}U\bigr)^{-1}VA^{-1}, \qquad(14)(A+UCV)−1=A−1−A−1U(C−1+VA−1U)−1VA−1,(14)

\Sigma_w = \Sigma_p - \Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigl(\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I} + \Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigr)^{-1}\Phi\Sigma_p. \qquad(15)Σw=Σp−ΣpΦ⊤(σn2𝐈+ΦΣpΦ⊤)−1ΦΣp.(15)

where the last step uses \sigma_n^{-2}(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}[(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})-K] = (K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}σn−2(K+σn2𝐈)−1[(K+σn2𝐈)−K]=(K+σn2𝐈)−1. Substituting these into the Gaussian predictive distribution from Equation 11 gives:
p(f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(f_* \;\middle|\; \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y},\; k(\mathbf{x}_*,\mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_* + \sigma_n^2\right). \qquad(17)p(f*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲)=𝒩(f*|𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲,k(𝐱*,𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*+σn2).(17)

The most important observation here is that \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟 has vanished entirely. The predictions clearly now depend purely on kernel evaluations between data points. We are free to specify kk directly, and we never need to construct an explicit feature map. In particular, if we allow M \to \inftyM→∞ many basis functions, and we define kk to be the corresponding inner product of this limit, then the model becomes non-parametric. The functions complexity grows with the data rather than being fixed in advance (Williams 1996; D. J. MacKay 1998). Williams (1996) showed that a Bayesian neural network with an infinite number of hidden units and a Gaussian weight prior converges to a GP, formally proving the connection between the weight-space and function-space views.

This is the so called function-space perspective. Instead of reasoning about a weight vector \mathbf{w}𝐰, we place a prior directly over functions, characterised entirely by kk. The result is a Gaussian process.

sec.title: 3. Gaussian Processes
sec.p:
Formally, a Gaussian process is a collection of random variables, any finite number of which have a joint Gaussian distribution (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). A GP is fully specified by its mean function m(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})]m(𝐱)=𝔼[f(𝐱)] and covariance function (or kernel)
k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \mathbb{E}[(f(\mathbf{x}) - m(\mathbf{x}))(f(\mathbf{x}') - m(\mathbf{x}'))] = \operatorname{Cov}[f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}')] \qquad(18)k(𝐱,𝐱′)=𝔼[(f(𝐱)−m(𝐱))(f(𝐱′)−m(𝐱′))]=Cov[f(𝐱),f(𝐱′)](18)

We write f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)f∼𝒢𝒫(m,k) to denote that ff is a random function drawn from a GP with mean mm and kernel kk. The GP provides a prior directly over functions, rather than over a finite parameter vector as in the weight-space view of Section 2.4.

sec.title: 3.1 The GP Prior
sec.p:
Placing a GP prior on ff gives a “prior over functions”. Evaluating ff at any finite collection of inputs \mathbf{X} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n\}𝐗={𝐱1,…,𝐱n} gives a joint Gaussian over the corresponding function values \mathbf{f} = [f(\mathbf{x}_1), \ldots, f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^\top𝐟=[f(𝐱1),…,f(𝐱n)]⊤,
\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, K), \qquad(19)𝐟∣𝐗∼𝒩(𝐦,K),(19)

where [\mathbf{m}]_i = m(\mathbf{x}_i)[𝐦]i=m(𝐱i) and K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)Kij=k(𝐱i,𝐱j). This property that every finite-dimensional marginal is Gaussian is a defining characteristic of the process (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; Williams and Rasmussen 1995). In regression, it is standard practice to take m \equiv 0m≡0: the training targets can be centred by subtracting their mean, and any residual structure is captured by the kernel (D. J. MacKay 1998). However, non-zero mean functions can be useful for encoding strong prior beliefs about the function shape, such as a linear trend or periodicity (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, sec. 2.2).

sec.title: 3.2 Kernels and Covariance Functions
sec.p: All of the structure of the prior is encoded in the kernel kk. The kernel determines how function values co-vary across input space: inputs that are ‘close’, as measured by the kernel kk, will have strongly correlated function values, while distant inputs are nearly independent. Kernel hyper-parameters directly control the interpretable properties such as the length-scale (how rapidly the function varies), the output scale (the typical amplitude), and whether the function is stationary or periodic. Figure 1 illustrates this with two common choices: the squared exponential (SE) kernel, which produces infinitely differentiable functions whose roughness is controlled by a length-scale parameter \ellℓ, and the periodic kernel, whose period parameter pp fixes the repetition frequency of the sampled functions.

caption.p: Figure 1: Prior samples from GPs with the SE kernel (left) and the periodic kernel (right) under varying hyperparameters.

sec.p:
The SE kernel, which is interchangeably called the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, is defined as
k_{\text{SE}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|^2}{2\ell^2}\right), \qquad(20)kSE(𝐱,𝐱′)=σf2exp(−∥𝐱−𝐱′∥22ℓ2),(20)

and is the most widely used GP kernel in practice (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). A small \ellℓ allows the function to vary rapidly over short distances, producing rough wiggly samples, while a large \ellℓ enforces smoothly varying functions. The periodic kernel,
k_{\text{per}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\sin^2\!\left(\pi|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'|/p\right)}{\ell^2}\right), \qquad(21)kper(𝐱,𝐱′)=σf2exp(−2sin2(π|𝐱−𝐱′|/p)ℓ2),(21)
explicitly encodes a repeating structure with period pp, making it suitable for modelling seasonal or cyclical signals.

Other common kernels include the Matérn family, which has an additional smoothness parameter that controls the differentiability of the sampled functions, and the rational quadratic kernel, which can be seen as a scale mixture of SE kernels and can capture varying length-scales (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, secs. 4.2–4.3).

Kernels can also be combined — sums and products of valid kernels are themselves valid kernels — enabling the construction of structured priors that capture multiple scales or mixed behaviours (Schölkopf 2002).

sec.title: 3.3 Choosing Kernel Hyperparameters
sec.p: The kernel hyperparameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 (e.g. length-scale \ellℓ, output scale \sigma_f^2σf2, noise variance \sigma_n^2σn2) are not specified by the GP directly, and must be estimated from data. The standard approach is to maximise the log marginal likelihood (LML) of the observed data under the GP model, which is known as type-II or level-II maximum likelihood or sometimes as empirical Bayes (D. J. C. MacKay 1992; D. J. MacKay 1998; Deisenroth 2010),

This LML has three interpretable terms: the first encourages the model to fit the data well, the second penalises overly complex models that can fit many functions, and the third is a constant that ensures the likelihood is properly normalised. The LML is typically maximised using gradient-based optimisation (e.g. L-BFGS or Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015)), which is tractable for exact GPs since the LML and its gradients can be computed in \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) time via Cholesky decomposition of K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}K+σn2𝐈 (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). However, the LML is non-convex and can have multiple local optima, so it is common to perform multiple random restarts to increase the chances of finding a good solution. Additionally, since kernel hyperparameters are typically constrained to be positive, as a negative length-scale or noise variance would not make sense, it is standard practice to optimise them in log-space to ensure positivity and improve numerical stability.

The posterior variance k_{\text{post}}(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*)kpost(𝐱*,𝐱*) is the prior variance at \mathbf{x}_*𝐱* minus a positive term that captures how much information about f(\mathbf{x}_*)f(𝐱*) is contained in the training data. As more data are observed near \mathbf{x}_*𝐱*, this reduction grows and uncertainty falls. Note that \sigma_n^2σn2 enters both posterior expressions through (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}(K+σn2𝐈)−1: noisier observations are down-weighted, so the posterior retains more prior uncertainty. The full predictive distribution for a new noisy observation y_* = f(\mathbf{x}_*) + \epsilon_*y*=f(𝐱*)+ϵ* adds +\sigma_n^2+σn2 to the latent posterior variance, giving Equation 24.

sec.title: 3.5 Training a GP
sec.p: We showed in Section 3.3 that the kernel hyper-parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 can be estimated by maximising the log marginal likelihood (LML) of the observed data. The LML is a non-convex function of \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉, but its gradients can be computed efficiently using matrix calculus and automatic differentiation, enabling gradient-based optimisation methods such as L-BFGS or Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) to find good hyperparameter settings. However, computing the LML and its gradients requires an \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}K+σn2𝐈, which is tractable for moderate nn but becomes prohibitive for large datasets, motivating the development of sparse and approximate inference methods for scaling GPs to larger problems (Snelson and Ghahramani 2006; Titsias 2009).

sec.title: 3.5.1 Gradient of the Log Marginal Likelihood
sec.p: We have the LML expression from Equation 22: \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\log |K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}| - \frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi.logp(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)=−12𝐲⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲−12log|K+σn2𝐈|−n2log2π.

The gradient of the LML with respect to a hyperparameter \theta_jθj can be derived using the matrix derivative trace formula (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, Equation 5.9), yielding: \frac{\partial \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \frac{\partial (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})}{\partial \theta_j} (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\text{tr}\!\left((K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \frac{\partial (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})}{\partial \theta_j}\right). ∂logp(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)∂θj=12𝐲⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1∂(K+σn2𝐈)∂θj(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲−12tr((K+σn2𝐈)−1∂(K+σn2𝐈)∂θj).

This expression consists of two terms: the first encourages the model to fit the data well by increasing the LML when the hyperparameter leads to a better fit, while the second penalises overly complex models by decreasing the LML when the hyperparameter increases model complexity. These gradients can be computed efficiently using automatic differentiation libraries, allowing for effective optimisation of the hyperparameters.

In practice, the training loop iterates: (1) evaluate the negative LML via Cholesky factorisation of K_\theta + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}Kθ+σn2𝐈; (2) backpropagate to obtain \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta_j∂ℒ/∂θj for each hyperparameter; (3) apply an update step (e.g. Adam). Because the LML is non-convex, running multiple random restarts and keeping the solution with the lowest negative LML is common practice. Positive-constrained hyperparameters (\ellℓ, \sigma_f^2σf2, \sigma_n^2σn2) are parameterised in log-space throughout to ensure positivity and improve the conditioning of the optimisation landscape. Figure 3 illustrates the effect of training: a GP with a poorly initialised length-scale produces an oversmoothed, miscalibrated fit, while the same model after 50 Adam steps accurately recovers the latent function.

Centre: negative log marginal likelihood during 50 Adam iterations. Right: GP after training — the learnt hyperparameter values are shown in the subtitle.

sec.title: 3.6 Prediction {#sec-gp-prediction} /TODO: CLEAN UP THIS SECTION
sec.p: With hyperparameters fixed at their optimised values \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}𝛉̂, prediction reduces to evaluating the posterior from Equation 25 at any desired test location \mathbf{x}_*𝐱*. The main cost for a prediciton is forming the Cholesky factorisation LL^\top = K_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}LL⊤=K𝛉̂+σn2𝐈, which is \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) and performed once. Once cached, evaluating the predictive mean and variance at a new point requires only two triangular solves and a kernel evaluation, costing \mathcal{O}(n)𝒪(n) per point. Therefore, making prediction at test time once training has been completed is efficient, and the main bottleneck is purely the training phase for large datasets.

The predictive variance at a test point \mathbf{x}_*𝐱* decomposes naturally into two parts:
\operatorname{Var}[y_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}, \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}] = \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_*}_{\text{epistemic (reducible)}} + \underbrace{\sigma_n^2}_{\text{aleatoric (irreducible)}}, \qquad(26)Var[y*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲,𝛉̂]=k(𝐱*,𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*⏟epistemic (reducible)+σn2⏟aleatoric (irreducible),(26)

where the first term is the epistemic uncertainty — reflecting ignorance about the latent function ff — and the second is the aleatoric noise variance (Kendall and Gal 2017). The epistemic component shrinks as training observations accumulate near \mathbf{x}_*𝐱*, and recovers the full prior variance k(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*)k(𝐱*,𝐱*) only in regions with no data. The aleatoric term \sigma_n^2σn2 is present whenever a noisy observation y_* = f(\mathbf{x}_*) + \epsilon_*y*=f(𝐱*)+ϵ* is requested, but absent from the latent predictive distribution over f(\mathbf{x}_*)f(𝐱*) itself. This separation is a distinctive strength of the GP framework: the two sources of uncertainty are quantified separately and automatically, without requiring any post-hoc calibration (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; Kendall and Gal 2017).

This is visible in Figure 2: uncertainty collapses near the training observations (low epistemic uncertainty) and inflates in the gaps and at the extrapolation boundaries (high epistemic uncertainty), while the posterior mean threads through the data.

sec.title: 4. Deep Gaussian Processes
sec.p: The previous section shows how GPs provide closed-form predictions and uncertainty estimates, and are entirely described by the choice of kernel. However, the expressiveness of a single-layer GP is fundamentally constrained by this. A stationary kernel like the squared exponential encodes a fixed idea of smoothness across the entire input space, which may not match real-world data where patterns and smoothness of data may vary in complexity across different regions.

Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) address this by composing multiple GP layers hierarchically. Rather than relying on a single kernel, DGPs learn representations at multiple levels of abstraction, much like deep neural networks, while retaining Bayesian uncertainty quantification. This section formally describes the DGP model and shows why exact inference becomes intractable. This leads into the approximate methods of Section 5.

sec.title: 4.1 Definition and Model Formulation
sec.p: DGPs extend standard GPs by composing multiple GP layers in a hierarchical structure (Damianou and Lawrence 2013). Instead of a single mapping from inputs to outputs, DGPs construct a chain of latent function spaces, each transforming the previous layer.
An LL-layer DGP is defined by a sequence of latent functions \{f^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}{f(ℓ)}ℓ=1L where each function is drawn from a GP prior conditioned on the output of the previous:

with the convention \mathbf{F}^{(0)} = \mathbf{X}𝐅(0)=𝐗 (the observed inputs). Each layer applies a freshly drawn GP function to the outputs of the previous layer — the first layer warps the raw inputs, the second warps those warped values, and so on. The model is a learned chain of transformations, each inheriting all the uncertainty of the layers before it.
For observed inputs \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_0}𝐗∈ℝn×d0 and outputs \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐲∈ℝn, the generative model proceeds as:

alternatives.tex-math: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}^{(1)} &= f^{(1)}(\mathbf{X}), & f^{(1)} &\sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k^{(1)}), \\ \mathbf{F}^{(2)} &= f^{(2)}(\mathbf{F}^{(1)}), & f^{(2)} &\sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k^{(2)}), \\ &\vdots \\ \mathbf{F}^{(L)} &= f^{(L)}(\mathbf{F}^{(L-1)}), & f^{(L)} &\sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k^{(L)}), \\ \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{F}^{(L)} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, & \boldsymbol{\epsilon} &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}), \end{aligned} \qquad(28)

sec.p: where \mathbf{F}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_\ell}𝐅(ℓ)∈ℝn×dℓ contains function evaluations at layer \ellℓ for all nn data points, and d_\elldℓ is the output dimensionality of layer \ellℓ.
The covariance matrix at layer \ellℓ is constructed from kernel evaluations at the random outputs of the previous layer:

where \mathbf{f}_i^{(\ell-1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell-1}}𝐟i(ℓ−1)∈ℝdℓ−1 is the ii-th row of \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1). When conditioned on the outputs from layer \ell-1ℓ−1, the distribution of \mathbf{F}^{(\ell)}𝐅(ℓ) remains multivariate Gaussian:

When \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) is held fixed, this is identical to a standard GP prior — layer \ellℓ behaves exactly like a regular GP evaluated at those inputs. The difficulty arises only when \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) is random: the covariance matrix K^{(\ell)}K(ℓ) then becomes a random variable itself, and integrating over it no longer yields a closed form.
The directed graph structure implies that each layer depends only on its immediate predecessor (a Markov property), leading to a factorised joint prior:

This follows from applying the chain rule and noting that \mathbf{F}^{(\ell)} \perp \mathbf{F}^{(1:\ell-2)}, \mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ)⟂𝐅(1:ℓ−2),𝐗∣𝐅(ℓ−1). In plain terms: once you know what layer \ell\!-\!1ℓ−1 output, knowledge of all earlier layers gives no additional information about layer \ellℓ. Practically, this means one can sample through the model one layer at a time, discarding each layer’s outputs once they have been passed forward. The likelihood connects the final layer to observations via p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{F}^{(L)}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{F}^{(L)}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I})p(𝐲∣𝐅(L))=𝒩(𝐲∣𝐅(L),σn2𝐈).
Equivalently, defining the composed function f = f^{(L)} \circ f^{(L-1)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}f=f(L)∘f(L−1)∘⋯∘f(1):
When layers have output dimension d_\ell > 1dℓ>1, the standard approach uses independent GPs per output dimension:
This leads to \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} n \cdot d_\ell = O(nLd)∑ℓ=1Ln⋅dℓ=O(nLd) total latent variables.

Figure 4 illustrates the compositional structure of a two-layer DGP. The first layer warps the input, and the second layer operates on the warped space, producing a composed function that would be difficult to represent with a single GP.

Centre: the second-layer function f^{(2)}f(2) maps the warped inputs to outputs. Right: the composed function f^{(2)} \circ f^{(1)}f(2)∘f(1) exhibits non-stationary behaviour — smooth in some regions and rapidly varying in others — that neither layer alone could produce.

sec.p: The expressiveness of DGPs over standard GPs comes from this composition (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Dunlop et al. 2018). Even when each layer uses a stationary kernel, the composed function yields a non-stationary process. Consider the covariance of g = f^{(2)} \circ f^{(1)}g=f(2)∘f(1):

This expectation depends on marginal distributions of f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x})f(1)(𝐱) and f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}')f(1)(𝐱′), which change with \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'𝐱,𝐱′ through k^{(1)}k(1). The composed covariance is therefore not simply a function of \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'𝐱−𝐱′, making the process non-stationary. This input-dependent structure lets DGPs model functions with varying smoothness and lengthscale across input space. To see why this is useful, imagine fitting a signal that is smooth in some regions and rapidly varying in others: a single GP with a fixed lengthscale must compromise, while a DGP can learn to “stretch” the input space in smooth regions and “compress” it in complex regions through f^{(1)}f(1), giving the second layer an effectively adapted coordinate system. sec.title: 4.2 Intractability of Exact Inference
sec.p: For standard single-layer GPs, the posterior p(f_* \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y})p(f*∣𝐗,𝐲) and marginal likelihood p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X})p(𝐲∣𝐗) give closed-form expressions due to Gaussian conjugacy (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). In DGPs this is lost because composition of GPs produces a non-Gaussian joint distribution.
The marginal likelihood requires integrating out all latent functions:

where \mathbf{F}^{(0)} = \mathbf{X}𝐅(0)=𝐗. This integral has no closed-form solution for L \geq 2L≥2 with non-degenerate kernels. The fundamental obstacle is that the covariance matrix K^{(\ell)}K(ℓ) at each layer is a nonlinear function of \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) — the very variables being integrated over — so the integral cannot be reorganised into the product-of-Gaussians form that makes single-layer GP inference tractable.

To see why, consider a two-layer DGP. The covariance matrix K^{(2)}K(2) depends on \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) through [K^{(2)}]_{ij} = k^{(2)}(f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})[K(2)]ij=k(2)(fi(1),fj(1)). For the squared exponential kernel:
this is a nonlinear function of the Gaussian random variables (f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})(fi(1),fj(1)). The integral

is a mixture of Gaussians with continuously varying covariance. Intuitively, for every possible realisation of \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) there is a different Gaussian over \mathbf{F}^{(2)}𝐅(2); marginalising out \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) means averaging together infinitely many Gaussians with different shapes, producing a result that is heavier-tailed and more complex than any individual Gaussian component. No closed form exists for these integrals.

As well as the intractability of the marginal likelihood, the resulting distribution over outputs is non-Gaussian. Consider a two-layer DGP with first-layer outputs h_1 = f^{(1)}(x_1)h1=f(1)(x1), h_2 = f^{(1)}(x_2)h2=f(1)(x2). From the GP prior:

alternatives.tex-math: \begin{bmatrix} h_1 \\ h_2 \end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(1)}_{11} & k^{(1)}_{12} \\ k^{(1)}_{12} & k^{(1)}_{22} \end{bmatrix}\right). \qquad(37)

sec.p: Conditioned on (h_1, h_2)(h1,h2), the outputs follow:

alternatives.tex-math: \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} \Bigg| h_1, h_2 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(2)}(h_1, h_1) & k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) \\ k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) & k^{(2)}(h_2, h_2) \end{bmatrix}\right). \qquad(38)

sec.p: The marginal distribution
is a continuous mixture of Gaussians with varying covariance matrices. Since k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2)k(2)(h1,h2) is a nonlinear function of (h_1, h_2)(h1,h2), this mixture is not Gaussian.

This can be verified by noting that a Gaussian mixture with continuously varying covariance matrices produces a distribution whose higher moments (e.g., kurtosis) differ from those of any single Gaussian. In particular, the marginal density of y_1y1 under such a mixture is generally heavier-tailed than any individual Gaussian component (Gelman et al. 2025).
The posterior over all latent functions is:
Since both the numerator (a product of coupled Gaussians) and the denominator (the intractable marginal likelihood) lack closed forms, exact posterior computation is infeasible.

Even numerical integration is impractical. The integration is over \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} n d_\ell∑ℓ=1Lndℓ continuous variables, which cannot be factored across layers due to kernel dependencies. This motivates the development of approximate inference methods for DGP learning (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017).

sec.title: 5. Learning in GP and DGP Models
sec.p: The previous section showed that DGPs offer richer modelling capacity than standard GPs, but at the cost of tractable inference. This section develops the framework for learning in both settings.

We briefly revisit hyperparameter learning in standard GPs — focusing on how the marginal likelihood arises by integrating out function values — to identify the structural property that is lost in DGPs. We then introduce variational inference for approximating intractable posteriors, build to sparse variational methods that reduce computation from O(n^3)O(n3) to O(nm^2)O(nm2), and finally extend these ideas to DGPs through doubly stochastic variational inference.

sec.title: 5.1 Learning in Standard GPs
sec.p: As established in Section 3.3, GP hyperparameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 are learned by maximising the log marginal likelihood (LML). It is worth seeing explicitly how this LML arises by integrating out the latent function values \mathbf{f}𝐟, since this tractability is precisely what is lost in DGPs.

Starting from the GP prior \mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})𝐟∣𝐗∼𝒩(𝟎,K𝛉) and likelihood \mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{f} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{f}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I})𝐲∣𝐟∼𝒩(𝐟,σn2𝐈), Gaussian–Gaussian conjugacy (Bernardo and Smith 2000) allows the integral over function values to be computed in closed form:
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \int p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{f}) p(\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d\mathbf{f} = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{0}, K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}), \qquad(41)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)=∫p(𝐲∣𝐟)p(𝐟∣𝐗,𝛉)d𝐟=𝒩(𝐲∣𝟎,K𝛉+σn2𝐈),(41) giving the LML of Equation 22. The key step is that a Gaussian prior on \mathbf{f}𝐟 multiplied by a Gaussian likelihood in \mathbf{y}𝐲 integrates analytically: the product of two Gaussians is proportional to a Gaussian, so the \mathbf{f}𝐟-integral collapses to a single multivariate normal with covariance K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}K𝛉+σn2𝐈. This closed-form collapse is precisely what is lost in DGPs, where the covariance depends on random latent variables. Hyperparameters are found via gradient ascent; the gradient with respect to \theta_jθj is (Rasmussen and Williams 2008):

where \boldsymbol{\alpha} = K_y^{-1} \mathbf{y}𝛂=Ky−1𝐲 and K_y = K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}Ky=K𝛉+σn2𝐈. The matrix \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top - K_y^{-1}𝛂𝛂⊤−Ky−1 has a natural interpretation: \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top𝛂𝛂⊤ is a rank-one outer product that captures how the data predicts itself under the current model, while K_y^{-1}Ky−1 reflects the full model uncertainty; a large positive difference for \partial K_y / \partial \theta_j∂Ky/∂θj indicates that increasing \theta_jθj improves the data fit more than it increases model complexity. This follows from the matrix calculus identities \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log|K| = \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta})∂∂θlog|K|=tr(K−1∂K∂θ) and \frac{\partial K^{-1}}{\partial \theta} = -K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta} K^{-1}∂K−1∂θ=−K−1∂K∂θK−1.

Each gradient step requires K_y^{-1}Ky−1, computed via Cholesky decomposition at O(n^3)O(n3) cost with O(n^2)O(n2) storage (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). For small to moderate datasets (n \lesssim 10{,}000n≲10,000) this is typically feasible and remains the gold standard: the LML gradients are exact, and no approximation is introduced beyond the choice of kernel. For larger datasets the cubic cost becomes prohibitive, motivating the sparse variational approach of the following section.

sec.title: 5.2 Variational Inference
sec.p: When exact inference is intractable, variational inference gives an approximation framework (Jordan et al. 1999; Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe 2017). The idea is to approximate the true posterior p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{y})p(𝐳∣𝐲) with a simpler, and tractable distribution q(\mathbf{z})q(𝐳), which is chosen to minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence between qq and pp:
For latent variables \mathbf{z}𝐳 and observations \mathbf{y}𝐲, the log marginal likelihood separates as:
where the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is:

Since KL divergence is non-negative, \mathcal{L}(q) \leq \log p(\mathbf{y})ℒ(q)≤logp(𝐲) with equality when q(\mathbf{z}) = p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{y})q(𝐳)=p(𝐳∣𝐲). This is the central insight: rather than computing the intractable posterior directly, we turn the problem into an optimisation — find the qq that maximises the ELBO, which simultaneously tightens the bound and minimises the error of our approximation.
To show Equation 43, start from the definition of KL divergence:

Rearranging gives Equation 43. Since \operatorname{KL}(q \| p)KL(q∥p) cannot be computed directly (it is intractable), we instead maximise the ELBO, which is equivalent to minimising KL divergence. This replaces an intractable posterior computation with a tractable optimisation problem — the core trade of variational inference.

The second form Equation 44 illuminates the ELBO’s structure. The expected log-likelihood \mathbb{E}_{q}[\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{z})]𝔼q[logp(𝐲∣𝐳)] encourages qq to concentrate where the data is well-explained, while the KL term \operatorname{KL}(q \| p(\mathbf{z}))KL(q∥p(𝐳)) regularises qq toward the prior, preventing overfitting (Bishop 2006). This trade-off mirrors the data-fit versus complexity balance in exact Bayesian inference.

For the models in this dissertation, variational inference serves two purposes: enabling scalability to large datasets, and handling the hierarchical structure of DGPs where function values at each layer cannot be analytically integrated out. The latent variables \mathbf{z}𝐳 correspond to function values \mathbf{f}𝐟, and the variational distribution is usually chosen to be Gaussian:

with variational parameters \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐦∈ℝn and S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}S∈ℝn×n (positive definite). This balances expressiveness with computational tractability. The expectations under qq can often be computed analytically for standard likelihood functions.
With this Gaussian choice, the KL term has closed form:

where KK is the prior covariance. Each term has a clear role: \mathbf{m}^\top K^{-1} \mathbf{m}𝐦⊤K−1𝐦 penalises the variational mean for straying far from zero in units of the prior length-scale; \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}S)tr(K−1S) penalises the variational covariance for being larger than the prior; and \log|K| - \log|S|log|K|−log|S| is a log-volume ratio that rewards qq for being more concentrated than the prior. Together they ensure qq cannot deviate from p(\mathbf{f})p(𝐟) without paying a KL cost. Optimisation over a full-rank matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}S∈ℝn×n still involves O(n^2)O(n2) parameters, which becomes problematic for large nn. The key to resolving this is to restrict the variational family to a lower-dimensional subspace defined by m \ll nm≪n inducing points, as developed in the following section.

sec.title: 5.3 Sparse Variational GPs
sec.p: The O(n^3)O(n3) cost of standard GP inference becomes prohibitive for large datasets. Sparse methods address this by using m \ll nm≪n inducing points that summarise the data, reducing complexity to O(nm^2)O(nm2) (Quinonero-Candela and Rasmussen 2005; Titsias 2009).

Consider inducing inputs \mathbf{Z} = \{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^m𝐙={𝐳j}j=1m with function values \mathbf{u} = f(\mathbf{Z}) \in \mathbb{R}^m𝐮=f(𝐙)∈ℝm. From the prior, the joint distribution of function values \mathbf{f}𝐟 at training inputs and inducing values \mathbf{u}𝐮 is:

where K_{ff} = K(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X})Kff=K(𝐗,𝐗), K_{fu} = K(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z})Kfu=K(𝐗,𝐙), and K_{uu} = K(\mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{Z})Kuu=K(𝐙,𝐙). The cross-covariance K_{fu}Kfu encodes how strongly each training point correlates with each inducing point: if inducing points are placed where the data concentrates, K_{fu}Kfu will be large and the mm inducing values will carry most of the information about the nn function values.

Titsias (2009) introduced a variational framework that treats \mathbf{Z}𝐙 as variational parameters rather than fixed pseudo-inputs. The key idea is to use the conditional p(\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{u})p(𝐟∣𝐮) from the prior and place a variational distribution on \mathbf{u}𝐮:

where q(\mathbf{u}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{u} \mid \mathbf{m}, S)q(𝐮)=𝒩(𝐮∣𝐦,S) with variational parameters \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^m𝐦∈ℝm and S \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}S∈ℝm×m. The variational distribution retains the form from Equation 57:

The term “doubly stochastic” refers to two sources of randomness: minibatch subsampling (stochasticity over data) and Monte Carlo sampling through layers (stochasticity over latent functions). Both maintain unbiasedness of gradient estimates, which is crucial for stochastic optimisation convergence. In practice the two sources of noise act independently: increasing the minibatch size |\mathcal{B}||ℬ| reduces noise from data sampling, while increasing the sample count SS reduces noise from layer propagation.

In effect, the randomness is “pushed outside” the computation graph, so automatic differentiation can treat \muμ and \sigmaσ as ordinary differentiable variables.

sec.title: 6. Deep Gaussian Processes for Financial Risk Modeling
sec.p: Gaussian processes are well-established Bayesian non-parametric models for regression and classification, and GP-based recurrent extensions have also been used for time-series modelling (Mattos et al. 2016). Deep Gaussian processes extend this framework by composing multiple GP layers, giving a more expressive probabilistic model while retaining an explicit treatment of predictive uncertainty (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017).

In finance, GP-based methods have been applied to credit-risk and credit-rating problems (Mahajan et al. 2022; Huang 2011), volatility forecasting (Munoz-Gonzalez, Lazaro-Gredilla, and Figueiras-Vidal 2014), algorithmic trading strategy identification (Yang et al. 2015), and market-risk approximation for trading portfolios (Lehdili, Oswald, and Nguyen 2025). Basel III and the wider Basel Framework make banks’ capital requirements explicitly risk-sensitive, so reliable estimates of probability of default (PD) and other loss-related quantities are important for both regulatory compliance and internal risk management (“Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011). Against that background, comparing GPs and DGPs for credit-risk prediction is well motivated. At the same time, the finance literature cited above is still dominated by standard GP variants, with direct DGP applications appearing much less common. Likely due to the regulatory issues around using black-box models in finance, and the computational challenges of training DGPs at scale, there is a gap in the literature around the practical performance of DGPs for financial risk modelling. This section therefore compares GPs and DGPs with standard machine learning baselines on financial datasets, focusing on both predictive performance and the quality of uncertainty quantification, while also considering computational cost and interpretability.

sec.title: 6.1 Credit Card Probability of Default
sec.p: The first empirical study addresses 2 question: can GP and DGP classifiers serve as credible probability-of-default (PD) models under realistic credit-risk conditions, and does the additional expressiveness of DGPs translate into superior performance relative to single-layer GPs and classical machine learning baselines for this data?

The benchmark used is the UCI default of credit card clients dataset (Yeh and Lien 2009), comprising 30,000 observations and 23 predictor variables: credit limit, demographics, six months of repayment-status history, and corresponding billing and repayment amounts from April–September 2005. The target indicates default on the October 2005 payment. This benchmark is well-established in the credit-risk literature (Thomas 2000; Huang 2011; Mahajan et al. 2022) and presents two simultaneous evaluation criteria: ranking quality discrimination ability (does the model correctly order clients by default risk?) and probability calibration (are the predicted default probabilities credible estimates of the observed default frequencies?). Under the Basel IRB Advanced Approach, both criteria carry legal and capital weight (“Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011; European Banking Authority 2017).

sec.title: 6.1.1 Data Preparation and Experimental Design
sec.p: Undocumented education and marriage codes were collapsed into an “other” category; skewed monetary variables (bill amounts and repayment amounts) were log-transformed to reduce leverage from extreme values; categorical variables were one-hot encoded with drop_first=True; and all continuous predictors were standardised to zero mean and unit variance fit on the training split only to prevent leakage (see Section 6.7.2 for the implementation). The full 30,000-observation dataset was first split into a fixed held-out test set of 6,000 observations (20%), due to large class imbalance this was stratified by the target variable to ensure equal default rates across train and test. The remaining 24,000 observations are used for training and validation subsets. This ensures all models across sizes are evaluated on the same test set, giving a fair comparison across training dataset sizes.
We evaluated three size tiers to study the effect of data quantity on performance:

sec.p: The model set comprises three classical tabular baselines and three GP-family models:

DSVGP-2L — two-layer deep sparse variational GP with doubly stochastic inference (Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017), 128 inducing points per layer, hidden dimension 5.
DSVGP-3L — three-layer variant of the above.

sec.title: 6.1.3.1 Discriminative Performance
sec.p: On threshold-independent ranking metrics, the six models form three tiers. XGBoost leads at ROC-AUC = 0.779 and average precision = 0.553, consistent with its strong performance on structured tabular data. The GP family follows closely: DSVGP-2L = 0.778, DSVGP-3L = 0.777, SVGP = 0.776 — a gap of \Delta = 0.001Δ=0.001–0.0030.003. Bootstrap 95% CIs span approximately \pm 0.015±0.015, and the intervals for XGBoost, DSVGP-2L, DSVGP-3L, and SVGP overlap completely: these four models are statistically indistinguishable on discrimination (Section 6.11). The point-estimate ordering within this group carries no weight. Random forest (0.769) and logistic regression (0.739) however do trail significantly. Logistic regression was worse, likely due to its inability to capture the non-linear interactions between repayment-status history and monetary variables that score highly on feature importance.

At each model’s F1-optimal threshold, the six models converge dramatically: SVGP achieves F1 = 0.547 at t^* = 0.30t*=0.30, DSVGP-2L = 0.546 at t^* = 0.29t*=0.29, XGBoost = 0.544 at t^* = 0.55t*=0.55, DSVGP-3L = 0.545 at t^* = 0.32t*=0.32, Random Forest = 0.542 at t^* = 0.47t*=0.47, and Logistic Regression = 0.519 at t^* = 0.58t*=0.58. The GP models’ lower optimal thresholds (0.29–0.32 versus 0.47–0.58 for classical models) reflect their characteristic narrower score distribution: the sigmoid-linked posterior concentrates predictions in a narrower probability band, requiring a lower cutoff to achieve the same sensitivity. This is not a deficiency — it is a direct consequence of the principled uncertainty quantification that also produces superior calibration.

sec.title: 6.1.3.2 Probability Calibration
sec.p: The principal advantage of GP and DGP classifiers on this dataset is probability calibration. SVGP achieves ECE = 0.015 and Brier = 0.136; DSVGP-3L: ECE = 0.016, Brier = 0.136; DSVGP-2L: ECE = 0.017, Brier = 0.135. Classical baselines are substantially worse: logistic regression ECE = 0.225, XGBoost ECE = 0.196, random forest ECE = 0.087. The GP models achieve approximately 12\times× lower ECE than XGBoost and 13\times× lower than logistic regression.

This pattern aligns with Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005), who show empirically that gradient-boosted ensembles are systematically overconfident while sigmoid-linked probabilistic models tend toward well-calibrated posteriors. The GP models are well-calibrated natively because the variational ELBO penalises over-confident posteriors and the Bernoulli-sigmoid link ensures appropriate uncertainty near the decision boundary (Hensman, Fusi, and Lawrence 2013).

Random forest occupies an intermediate position (ECE = 0.087): its bagging mechanism provides some calibration smoothing, but the frequency-based probability estimates from leaf nodes are still systematically biased relative to the Bayesian posterior of the GP family (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005).

Under the Basel IRB Advanced Approach, PD estimates must track observed default rates across rating grades (European Banking Authority 2017; “Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011). A raw ECE of 0.196 (XGBoost) implies average deviations of nearly 20 percentage points per quantile bin — a level that would fail a standard supervisory calibration review and distort IFRS 9 expected credit loss provisions (International Accounting Standards Board 2014). GP models satisfy this standard natively; classical models would require a post-hoc calibration stage (Platt scaling (Platt 1999) or isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan 2002)) that adds to both the data budget and the validation surface area under model risk frameworks such as SR 11-7 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System 2011). However, introducing a post-hoc calibration layer raises its own regulatory concerns: the calibration mapping is itself a model component that must be validated, monitored, and governed. In high-stakes applications such as IRB PD estimation, each additional model component increases the total validation burden and creates a potential point of failure during model monitoring. The GP’s native calibration avoids this additional complexity entirely.

sec.title: 6.1.4.1 Discriminative Scaling
sec.p: All models benefit from additional training data, but the magnitude and pattern of improvement differ across families.

Classical models. XGBoost shows the strongest scaling response: ROC-AUC improves from 0.734 (small) to 0.779 (large), a gain of +0.045. This is characteristic of gradient-boosted ensembles’ well-documented capacity to exploit large training sets through deeper tree structures and more refined split boundaries. Random forest improves more modestly (+0.023), and logistic regression shows the weakest response (+0.023), as a linear model that has already captured most of its achievable signal from the dominant repayment-status features at small scale.

GP models. SVGP improves from 0.744 to 0.776 (+0.032), while DSVGP-2L shows a comparable trajectory from 0.741 to 0.778 (+0.037). Both GP variants converge toward XGBoost at large scale: at the medium tier, DSVGP-2L (0.768) and SVGP (0.766) already match or exceed random forest (0.760), and the gap to XGBoost (0.758) has closed to within 0.01.

DSVGP-3L failure at small scale. The three-layer DGP achieves only ROC-AUC = 0.529 — effectively random — when trained on 425 observations. This is a clear instance of the pathological behaviour identified by Duvenaud et al. (2014), whereby deeper GP architectures suffer from vanishing kernel gradients and poor optimisation in the low-data regime. With only 425 training points and three layers of inducing-point variational parameters to optimise, the posterior collapses to a near-constant prediction. At medium scale (4,250 observations), DSVGP-3L recovers fully to 0.765, and at large scale it matches DSVGP-2L at 0.777. This demonstrates that the additional expressive capacity of deeper architectures requires sufficient data volume to be realised — a practical constraint that favours DSVGP-2L as the default configuration for credit-risk applications where training data may be limited.

sec.title: 6.1.4.2 Calibration Scaling
sec.p: The calibration behaviour across tiers reveals a qualitatively different pattern from discrimination.

GP models maintain excellent calibration at all scales. SVGP achieves ECE = 0.029 at small scale, improving to 0.011 at medium and settling at 0.015 at large. DSVGP-2L follows a similar trajectory (0.025 → 0.019 → 0.017). The key observation is that GP calibration quality is excellent from 425 training observations onward: an ECE of 0.025–0.029 represents average per-bin probability deviations of 2.5–2.9 percentage points, well within the tolerance of a supervisory PD calibration review (European Banking Authority 2017).

Classical models are miscalibrated at all scales and do not improve with more data. Logistic regression ECE is 0.205 at small scale and 0.225 at large — essentially constant. XGBoost ECE actually worsens from 0.164 (small) to 0.196 (large), as a more confidently fitted model produces more extreme probability estimates without a mechanism to pull them back toward calibration. Random forest is better calibrated than the other classicals (ECE \approx 0.09≈0.09 at all scales) due to the averaging effect of bagging, but still represents 5–6\times× worse calibration than the GP family.

This scaling pattern is a structural consequence of model architecture: GP models derive calibration from the Bayesian posterior’s principled treatment of uncertainty, which operates regardless of sample size (Bernardo and Smith 2000). Classical models derive their probability estimates from point-estimate decision functions (logit, tree leaf frequencies, boosted scores) that lack an inherent uncertainty calibration mechanism (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005).

sec.title: 6.1.5 Computational Profile

caption.p: Figure 7: Training time versus ECE for the six models at large scale. GP-family models provide substantially better native calibration at training times two to three orders of magnitude greater.
Table 4: Training time scaling across tiers. GP models scale approximately linearly with NN; DSVGP-3L is \sim 3.5\times∼3.5× the cost of DSVGP-2L at all scales.

sec.p: DSVGP-3L is the most expensive model at 582.8 seconds — nearly 3.5\times× the cost of the two-layer variant — yet yields no material improvement over DSVGP-2L on any metric at large scale (ROC-AUC: 0.777 vs 0.778; ECE: 0.016 vs 0.017). This is consistent with Duvenaud et al. (2014), who demonstrate that additional GP layers suppress rather than enhance flexibility on smooth finite datasets. DSVGP-2L is consequently the more defensible configuration: it achieves near-best discrimination, excellent calibration, and less than one-third the training cost of the three-layer variant.

For deployment contexts, the GP training time penalty (168 s for DSVGP-2L vs 0.58 s for XGBoost at large scale — a 290\times290× factor) is a batch training cost incurred once per model refresh cycle. In credit-risk production environments where models are retrained monthly or quarterly, this is operationally negligible. Inference time for a single prediction is comparable across model families.

sec.title: 6.1.6 Discussion
sec.p: Discriminative performance. At full scale, GP and DGP classifiers are competitive with gradient-boosted trees on all threshold-independent metrics, with ROC-AUC gaps of \Delta \leq 0.003Δ≤0.003 — smaller than the \pm 0.015±0.015 bootstrap CI width — meaning XGBoost and the GP family are statistically tied on discrimination (Section 6.11). At each model’s F1-optimal threshold, the GP family achieves the highest F1: SVGP = 0.547 versus XGBoost’s 0.544, eliminating the artefactual gap that appears when all models are evaluated at a fixed t = 0.5t=0.5 cutoff. The GP models’ lower optimal thresholds (0.29–0.32) versus classical models (0.47–0.58) reflect their narrower posterior score distributions — an expected consequence of principled Bayesian uncertainty quantification, not a modelling deficiency. In practice, this means that any deployment of these models must include a threshold selection step, ideally calibrated to the specific cost structure of the application (e.g., the relative cost of false positives vs false negatives in credit decisioning). Due to GPs much more accurate probability estimates, this threshold selection can be done purely off a chosen probability cutoff (e.g., 0.5) without needing to adjust for the model’s score distribution, which is a practical, and interpretability, advantage over classical baselines which would require a more complex threshold selection process or post-hoc calibration to achieve the same effect.

Probability calibration. The structural advantage of GP and DGP models on this task is native probability calibration. At large scale, the GP family achieves ECE = 0.015–0.017 compared to 0.087–0.225 for classical baselines — a 5–13\times× improvement requiring no additional calibration step, calibration data holdout, or post-hoc model component. This advantage is maintained across all training set sizes: even at small scale (425 training observations), GP models achieve ECE = 0.025–0.029, far superior to any classical baseline. For regulatory PD applications requiring credible default probability estimates under Basel IRB (European Banking Authority 2017) or IFRS 9 (International Accounting Standards Board 2014), this native calibration is a material operational advantage that eliminates both the calibration data tax and the additional validation surface imposed by post-hoc calibration methods (Platt 1999; Zadrozny and Elkan 2002).

Practical implications. These results carry both positive and cautionary messages for credit-risk practitioners. On the positive side, GP models deliver near-identical discriminative power to XGBoost while offering dramatically better calibration — the property that matters most for regulatory PD estimation. A bank adopting a GP-based PD model could expect regulatory capital calculations and IFRS 9 provisions that more accurately reflect true portfolio risk, reducing both the risk of supervisory challenge and the capital drag from over-conservative PD estimates. On the cautionary side, the training time premium (~290\times×) and the need for threshold optimisation add operational complexity. For portfolios where calibration quality is not subject to direct regulatory scrutiny (e.g., marketing scorecards), the simpler XGBoost pipeline may be preferable.

Architecture depth. Adding a third GP layer (DSVGP-3L) offers no benefit over DSVGP-2L at medium or large scale on any metric, while incurring approximately 3.5\times3.5× the training cost. At small scale, the three-layer architecture fails catastrophically (ROC-AUC = 0.529), confirming the practical relevance of the pathological deep GP behaviours identified by Duvenaud et al. (2014). DSVGP-2L is the dominant configuration across all training regimes for this dataset.

GP vs DGP. The marginal improvement from SVGP to DSVGP-2L is +0.002 ROC-AUC at large scale — not statistically significant given the \pm 0.015±0.015 CI width (Section 6.11), and below any threshold of practical relevance. This gap is modest relative to the 17% increase in training time (168 s vs 144 s). On calibration, both architectures achieve comparable ECE (\leq 0.02≤0.02). For this dataset, the single-layer SVGP provides approximately equivalent discriminative and calibration performance to the deep architecture at lower computational and optimisation risk. The additional compositional flexibility of DGPs (Damianou and Lawrence 2013) does not yield materially different representations on this smooth, moderate-dimensional credit dataset.

sec.title: 6.2 Freddie Mac Mortgage Probability of Default
sec.p: The second empirical study applies the same model set to a structurally different credit problem: residential mortgage probability of default. The data are drawn from the Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset, a publicly available supervisory-quality source covering origination characteristics and monthly loan performance for conforming mortgages purchased or guaranteed by Freddie Mac. This dataset is widely used in mortgage credit-risk research and regulatory stress-testing (“Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011) because it provides the granularity needed for loan-level PD modelling: origination credit score (FICO), combined loan-to-value (CLTV), debt-to-income ratio (DTI), original unpaid principal balance (UPB), coupon rate, loan purpose, property type, occupancy status, geographic region, and origination vintage.

The mortgage setting differs from the credit-card benchmark of Section 6.1 in three material respects. First, the default rate is far lower: approximately 1.7% versus 22.1%, making this a heavily imbalanced classification problem where the positive class is rare and most conventional threshold-dependent metrics become uninformative at any fixed cutoff. Second, the feature space includes structured domain covariates (FICO, LTV, DTI, vintage era, refinancing incentive) whose interactions are well-studied in the mortgage finance literature and carry direct economic interpretation. Third, the regulatory context is more demanding: mortgage PD models feed directly into Basel IRB capital calculations, IFRS 9 expected credit loss provisions, and CCAR/DFAST stress-testing submissions, where probability calibration is subject to direct supervisory scrutiny (European Banking Authority 2017; International Accounting Standards Board 2014; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System 2011).

sec.title: 6.2.1 Data Preparation and Experimental Design
sec.p: Origination and monthly performance files were loaded for all available quarters, retaining only those with at least 24 months of seasoning — the standard observation window for through-the-cycle PD estimation under Basel III (“Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011). A loan is labelled as defaulted if it reached 90+ days past due or experienced a credit-event liquidation (foreclosure, short sale, or related disposition) within 24 months of origination. This definition aligns with the Basel IRB default definition and is standard across the mortgage PD literature.

From the pool of qualifying origination records, a stratified subsample of 30,000 loans was drawn using proportional allocation across three stratification variables: vintage era (pre-crisis, crisis, post-crisis, COVID), refinancing incentive bucket (in-the-money, at-the-money, out-of-the-money based on rate spread relative to cohort median), and US Census geographic region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West). This stratified sampling preserves the portfolio-level distributional structure that drives mortgage default heterogeneity while reducing the dataset to a computationally manageable size.

Pre-processing followed the same conventions as Section 6.1. Categorical variables — loan purpose, property type, occupancy status, origination channel, first-time buyer flag, vintage era, refinancing bucket, LTV bucket, and geographic region — were one-hot encoded with drop_first=True to avoid the dummy-variable trap. Numeric covariates (credit score, original LTV, DTI, coupon rate, UPB, mortgage insurance percentage, rate spread, number of borrowers, number of units, original term, and origination year) were log-transformed where appropriate and standardised to zero mean and unit variance. The scaler was fit on training data only to prevent leakage.

The 30,000-loan sample was split into a fixed held-out test set of 6,000 observations (20%), stratified by the target. The remaining 24,000 observations form the development pool. Three training-set size tiers were evaluated:

list-item.p: Large (N_{\text{dev}} = 24{,}000Ndev=24,000): 20,400 training, 3,600 validation observations (full development set).

sec.p: The test set default rate is 1.73% across all tiers — approximately one-thirteenth the rate observed in the credit-card benchmark. This extreme class imbalance means that a naive majority-class classifier achieves 98.3% accuracy, rendering accuracy-based evaluation meaningless. The analysis therefore focuses on ROC-AUC for discrimination and ECE for calibration.

sec.title: 6.2.2 Model Set and Training Configuration
sec.p: The model set is identical to Section 6.1.2: logistic regression (class_weight="balanced"), random forest (500 trees, class_weight="balanced_subsample"), XGBoost (scale_pos_weight, early stopping on validation), SVGP (512 inducing points, 150 epochs), DSVGP-2L (128 inducing points per layer, hidden dimension 5), and DSVGP-3L.

The low default rate creates a specific challenge for threshold selection. At 1.73% base rate, a well-calibrated model should output probabilities near 0.017 for the majority of observations. The sigmoid-linked GP posterior naturally produces such concentrated estimates, meaning the predicted probability mass lies far below the conventional 0.50.5 threshold. At t = 0.5t=0.5, F1 is exactly zero for random forest, SVGP, DSVGP-2L, and DSVGP-3L across all tiers — these models correctly assign very low default probabilities to the overwhelmingly non-default majority, resulting in zero positive predictions at that cutoff. This makes using a fixed 0.50.5 threshold absurd for this dataset; even well-calibrated models that perfectly track the true 1.7% default rate would appear to “fail” at this cutoff. All threshold-dependent metrics below are therefore reported at each model’s F1-optimal threshold (t^*t*), which ranges from 0.02 to 0.81 depending on model and tier. Even at optimal thresholds, the best achievable F1 is approximately 0.15, reflecting the fundamental difficulty of achieving high precision and recall simultaneously at 1.73% prevalence. ROC-AUC, which evaluates the full ranking over all thresholds, is the appropriate primary metric. Statistical uncertainty in all metrics is quantified via 2,000-resample bootstrap confidence intervals (percentile method); see Section 6.11.

sec.title: 6.2.3.1 Discriminative Performance
sec.p: On the mortgage dataset, point estimates place DSVGP-3L first at ROC-AUC = 0.823, followed by DSVGP-2L = 0.821, logistic regression = 0.820, SVGP = 0.819, XGBoost = 0.785, and random forest = 0.774. However, with only \approx 104≈104 positive examples in the 6,000-observation test set (1.73% prevalence), bootstrap 95% CIs span approximately \pm 0.04±0.04 — and the intervals for all six models overlap substantially (Section 6.11). No pairwise ROC-AUC difference is statistically significant at this test-set size. The tentative two-tier pattern — GP/DGP family at 0.819–0.823 versus tree-based ensembles at 0.774–0.785 — is consistent across all four GP models and represents a reversal from the credit-card result where XGBoost led, consistent with the GP kernel’s smooth non-parametric structure better capturing the monotonic FICO/LTV/DTI risk relationships. Confirming this reversal would require a larger test set.

Logistic regression’s strong showing (ROC-AUC = 0.820, tied second with DSVGP-2L to three decimal places) is consistent with long-standing findings in the mortgage credit-risk literature, where simple scorecard-like linear models often perform competitively due to the approximately monotonic relationships between the primary risk drivers and default (Thomas 2000). However, as the calibration analysis below demonstrates, logistic regression’s discriminative adequacy masks severe probability estimation failures.

Average precision — a metric that gives more weight to correctly ranking positive examples and is thus sensitive to model quality in the rare-event tail — tells a clearer story of GP advantage: DSVGP-2L = 0.084, DSVGP-3L = 0.082, logistic regression = 0.081, SVGP = 0.079, random forest = 0.062, XGBoost = 0.059. The GP family consistently concentrates its ranking quality in the critical positive-class region.

On threshold-dependent F1, logistic regression leads at 0.153 (t^* = 0.81t*=0.81), followed by random forest at 0.143 (t^* = 0.24t*=0.24) and SVGP at 0.141 (t^* = 0.07t*=0.07). However, F1 values in the 0.13–0.15 range are inherently low for all models and reflect the fundamental difficulty of the task at 1.73% prevalence rather than meaningful performance differences. The spread of 0.025 between the best and worst F1 is far less informative than the ROC-AUC and calibration differences.

sec.title: 6.2.3.2 Probability Calibration
sec.p: The calibration advantage of GP and DGP models is dramatically amplified on the mortgage dataset relative to the credit-card benchmark. At a 1.73% base rate, small absolute errors in predicted probabilities translate to large relative distortions: a model that predicts 5% default probability when the true rate is 1.7% is overestimating risk by nearly 3\times3×, with direct capital cost implications under IRB.

DSVGP-2L achieves ECE = 0.002, SVGP = 0.003, DSVGP-3L = 0.004 — all effectively perfect calibration given the estimation uncertainty at this sample size. Random forest (ECE = 0.055) occupies a middling position, while logistic regression (ECE = 0.337) and XGBoost (ECE = 0.400) are severely miscalibrated. XGBoost’s ECE of 0.400 means that its predicted probabilities deviate from observed frequencies by an average of 40 percentage points per quantile bin — an order-of-magnitude failure that makes its raw probability outputs unusable for PD estimation without extensive post-hoc calibration.

The GP family achieves ECE values approximately 100\times× lower than XGBoost (0.003 vs 0.400) and 170\times× lower than logistic regression (0.002 vs 0.337). These ratios are far larger than the 12–13\times× advantage seen on the credit-card dataset, demonstrating that the calibration benefit of the Bayesian posterior is proportionally greater when the true event rate is low. At a 1.73% base rate, the sigmoid-linked GP posterior correctly concentrates prediction mass near the base rate with appropriate uncertainty, while classical models’ point-estimate decision functions produce scores that are poorly aligned with the rare-event target distribution.

The Brier score and log loss reinforce this picture. GP models achieve Brier = 0.016–0.017 and log loss = 0.075–0.076, while classical baselines range from 0.023–0.186 (Brier) and 0.114–0.555 (log loss). The GP log loss is approximately 7\times7× lower than XGBoost’s, reflecting the severe penalty that the logarithmic scoring rule imposes on confident but incorrect probability predictions (Bernardo and Smith 2000).

Under Basel IRB, PD estimates must track observed default rates within rating-grade buckets, and regulators increasingly validate calibration through ECE-like tests (European Banking Authority 2017). An ECE of 0.400 (XGBoost) or 0.337 (logistic regression) would fail any reasonable supervisory calibration standard. In contrast, GP models with ECE \leq 0.004≤0.004 produce probability estimates that are directly usable for regulatory capital calculation, IFRS 9 provisions (International Accounting Standards Board 2014), and stress-testing submissions without requiring a post-hoc calibration stage, which itself introduces additional model risk under SR 11-7 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System 2011).

The question of whether post-hoc calibration could close this gap for classical models is important. Platt scaling (Platt 1999) or isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan 2002) could potentially improve the ECE of XGBoost and logistic regression. However, this introduces three practical concerns: (1) the calibration mapping requires a held-out calibration set, reducing the training budget available for the base model; (2) the calibration layer is itself a model component that must be independently validated, governed, and monitored under supervisory frameworks such as SR 11-7 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System 2011); and (3) for low-default portfolios where positive examples are scarce, the calibration set may contain too few defaults to reliably fit the calibration mapping. GP models avoid all three concerns by providing native calibration from the Bayesian posterior.
